newsitem.title: UK: Dollar up in late Europe, awaits US vote result.
newsitem.headline: Dollar up in late Europe, awaits US vote result.

text.p: The dollar was firmer in late Europe against the mark and yen but turnover was subdued as the market awaited the results of U.S. presidential and key congressional elections.
"We know Clinton will be the future U.S. president, but the key is who will control Congress," said a Geneva-based trader.
In Moscow, the Kremlin said Russian President Boris Yeltsin's seven-hour open heart surgery had been a "complete success.'
While the dollar was unimpressed, the Swiss franc, a traditional safe-haven currency, took a slight hit on the news.
Traders said the slide in Swiss franc against the mark, which slid to 20-month lows of 84.18 centimes per mark on Tuesday, could have helped drag up dollar/mark.
The dollar was quoted at 1.5180/85 marks by 1626 GMT, against Monday's European close at 1.5140/47 marks.

While currency markets had seemed to discount the re-election of Bill Clinton and maintained control of Congress, the dollar picked up steam as U.S. asset markets jumped, convinced the Republican party will maintain its slim margin of control in Congress.
Analysts said the dollar focus should now fall on the U.S. quarterly refunding.

The U.S. quarterly refunding or auction of government debt started on Tuesday with an offer of $18.5 billion worth of three-year notes. On Wednesday $10 billion worth of 10-year notes will be offered while on Thursday $10 billion worth of 30-year bonds will be offered.
"Attention has been re-focused to the quarterly refunding," said Stuart Thompson, chief international economist at Nikko Europe.
But the major Japanese life insurance companies are not expected to be big players in the U.S. quarterly refunding ahead of the U.S. vote result.

Thompson said because Japanese investors have perhaps been more concerned about the risk of a Democrat victory in the U.S. Congress, they have, more than others, held off their purchases of overseas assets temporarily.
"Once the election is out of the way, I think you will see the dollar trending back to the 115 (yen) level," said Thompson.
Dollar/yen at 1656 GMT was trading at 114.10/4.20 against 113.90/4.00 in late Europe on Thursday.
Traders said dollar/mark also picked up steam following soft German data, which threw cold water on recent speculation of a hike in German rates.
"The data tended to undermine the Deutsche mark," said one trader.
A sharp 3.6 percent fall in German industry orders for September came hard on the heels of Monday's unexpected 1.8 percent drop in September industrial output.

"German manufacturing orders came out much softer than expected and will tend to keep a cap on the upside for the mark and expectations about the German economy," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economic adviser at Bank of America here.
